Focus on 4 things now: the firm, technical fit, behavioral stories, and questions to ask. Do these in order; I list exact practice prompts and a 10-point mini plan you can run through in 60–90 minutes.

1) Quick firm facts to have ready (2–3 lines each you should fill)
- What Lincoln International does: [one-line summary of the firm in your words].
- Why you want Lincoln: [your 1–2 sentence reason].
- A recent deal or sector focus: [name a deal or sector and the role you’d play as an analyst on it].
2) Technical prep (expect finance + modeling + deal workflow)
- Review: LBO mechanics (sources & uses, debt tranches, IRR math), 3-statement linking, and working-capital impacts. Have one short example of a lever that changes IRR and why: [your example].
- Walkthrough: be able to build (or verbally outline) a 5-minute DCF: revenue growth assumptions, margin progression to NOPAT, capex vs. D&A, WACC, terminal value method and sensitivity table.
- Accounting: explain a change in NWC affect on cash flow, and a basic capex vs. expense distinction.
Practice prompts:
- “Walk me through a DCF.”
- “How does an acquisition affect the acquirer’s balance sheet?”
- Quick calculations: given EBITDA, multiple, and net debt — what’s enterprise value, equity value, per-share impact? (Practice one example you choose: [example numbers]).
3) Behavioral / fit stories — use short STARs with numbers
Prepare 4 crisp stories (30–90 seconds each). For each, name the situation, your action with specifics, and a measurable result.
- Lead on analysis under a tight deadline: [situation, action, result].
- Found an error in a model or analysis: [situation, action, result].
- Worked in a small team / supported senior deal leads: [situation, action, result].
- Handled conflicting priorities / pressure: [situation, action, result].
I can mock one now and score it; tell me which story you want to practice first.
4) Case / modeling test prep
- If they give a live model or case, clarify assumptions first and say them aloud: revenue growth by segment, margins, capex schedule, tax rate, working-capital days.
- Speak your steps: “I’ll build revenue, margin, then link to cash flow and run sensitivity on exit multiple and margin.” Say checkpoints aloud every 5 minutes.
- If time-limited, prioritize a clean 3-year P&L and a simple terminal value to show you can reach a sensible valuation.
5) Questions to ask them (pick 3, one from each group)
About the deal/role:
- “What types of deals would I work on in the first 6–12 months?”  
About training & team:
- “How do analysts typically develop at Lincoln and what training or templates will I get?”  
About culture & expectations:
- “What does success look like for an analyst in the first year?”  
Reserve one technical question to show depth: “How does the team typically model working-capital seasonality for [sector]?” (fill [sector]).
6) Common final-round pitfalls — avoid these
- Don’t ramble: answer with structure (one-line situation, two actions, one result).
- Don’t over-quantify without basis: if you guess a number, call it an estimate.
- Don’t be passive in case work: narrate your thinking and trade-offs.
7) One-pass 60–90 minute rehearsal plan (do this now)
- 0–10 min: firm + role statements; pick your reason for joining Lincoln and write it as one sentence: [your reason].
- 10–30 min: run through DCF + LBO walkthroughs aloud (one each).
- 30–50 min: write and refine your 4 [your skill] stories to be 30–90s each.
- 50–70 min: mock technical Q&A — I ask “Walk me through a DCF” then “How does an acquisition affect the acquirer’s balance sheet?”
- 70–90 min: mock behavioral — pick two stories; I score and give one concrete fix each.

I can run the mock now. Choose: technical question first or behavioral/story practice first? Is that right?
